landmarks.name: Mount Fuji
landmarks.writeup: An iconic stratovolcano and Japan's highest peak, revered for its symmetrical cone and cultural significance.

wiki.extract: Mount Fuji  is an active stratovolcano located on the Japanese island of Honshu, with a summit elevation of 3,776.24 m. It is the highest mountain in Japan, the second-highest volcano on any Asian island, and the seventh-highest peak of an island on Earth. Mount Fuji last erupted from 1707 to 1708.

landmarks.name: Tokyo Tower
landmarks.writeup: A communications and observation tower in Tokyo, symbolizing Japan's post-war rebirth and modernization.

wiki.extract: Tokyo Skytree , a.k.a Tokyo Sky Tree, is a broadcasting and observation tower, located in Sumida, Tokyo, Japan. It has been the tallest tower in Japan since opening in 2012, and reached its full height of 634 metres in early 2011, making it the tallest tower in the world, displacing the Canton Tower, and the third tallest structure in the world behind Merdeka 118 and Burj Khalifa.

landmarks.name: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
landmarks.writeup: A Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto famous for its stunning gold leaf exterior and serene garden setting.

wiki.extract: Kinkaku-ji , officially named Rokuon-ji , is a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan and a tourist attraction. It is designated as a World Heritage Site, a National Special Historic Site, a National Special Landscape, and one of the 17 Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto. The temple is nicknamed after its reliquary (shariden), the Golden Pavilion , whose top two floors are coated in 0.5 μm gold leaf. The current pavilion was rebuilt in 1955 after being destroyed in an arson attack.

landmarks.name: Himeji Castle
landmarks.writeup: A well-preserved feudal castle known for its elegant white appearance and complex defensive design.

wiki.extract: Himeji Castle  is a hilltop Japanese castle complex situated in Himeji, a city in Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan. The castle is regarded as the finest surviving example of prototypical Japanese castle architecture, comprising a network of 83 structures with advanced defensive systems from the feudal period. The castle is frequently known as Hakuro-jō or Shirasagi-jō because of its brilliant white exterior and supposed resemblance to a bird taking flight.

landmarks.name: Itsukushima Shrine
landmarks.writeup: A Shinto shrine on Miyajima Island, renowned for its 'floating' torii gate visible at high tide.

wiki.extract: Itsukushima Shrine  is a Shinto shrine on the island of Itsukushima, best known for its "floating" torii. It is in the city of Hatsukaichi, in Hiroshima Prefecture in Japan, accessible from the mainland by ferry at Miyajimaguchi Station. The shrine complex is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Japanese government has designated several buildings and possessions as National Treasures.

cultural_events.name: Cherry Blossom Festival (Hanami)
cultural_events.writeup: A springtime celebration where people gather to view and appreciate the blooming cherry blossoms.

wiki.extract: Hanami  is the Japanese traditional custom of enjoying the transient beauty of flowers; flowers  in this case almost always mean those of the cherry  or, less frequently, plum  trees. From the end of March to early May, cherry trees bloom all over Japan, and around the second week of January on the island of Okinawa. The blossom forecast "cherry blossom front" is announced each year by the Japan Meteorological Agency and watched carefully by those planning hanami, as the blossoms only last a week or two.

cultural_events.name: Gion Matsuri
cultural_events.writeup: One of Japan's most famous festivals held in Kyoto, featuring elaborate floats and traditional processions.

wiki.extract: The Gion Festival  is one of the largest and most famous festivals in Japan, taking place annually during the month of July in Kyoto. Many events take place in central Kyoto and at the Yasaka Shrine, the festival's patron shrine, located in Kyoto's famous Gion district, which gives the festival its name. It is formally a Shinto festival, and its original purposes were purification and pacification of disease-causing entities. There are many ceremonies held during the festival, but it is best known for its two Yamaboko Junkō (山鉾巡行) processions of floats, which take place on July 17 and 24.

cultural_events.name: Obon Festival
cultural_events.writeup: A Buddhist event honoring the spirits of ancestors with dances, ceremonies, and family reunions.

wiki.extract: Obon  or just Bon  is a fusion of the ancient Japanese belief in ancestral spirits and a Japanese Buddhist custom to honor the spirits of one's ancestors. This syncretic folk Buddhist custom has evolved into a family reunion holiday during which people return to ancestral family places and visit and clean their ancestors' graves when the spirits of ancestors are supposed to revisit the household altars. It has been celebrated in Japan for more than 500 years and traditionally includes a dance, known as Bon Odori.

cultural_events.name: Tanabata
cultural_events.writeup: A festival celebrating the meeting of two deities, marked by colorful decorations and wish writing.

wiki.extract: Tanabata , also known as the Star Festival , is a Japanese festival originating from the Chinese Qixi Festival. It celebrates the meeting of the deities Orihime and Hikoboshi. According to legend, the Milky Way separates these lovers, and they are allowed to meet only once a year on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month of the lunisolar calendar. The date of Tanabata varies by region of the country, but the first festivities begin on 7 July of the Gregorian calendar. The celebration is held at various days between July and August.

food_writeup: Japanese cuisine emphasizes seasonal ingredients, presentation, and balance, featuring dishes like sushi, ramen, tempura, and sashimi, reflecting a deep cultural appreciation for freshness and aesthetics.
brief_history: Japan's history spans from ancient Jomon culture through feudal samurai eras, isolationist policies in the Edo period, rapid modernization during the Meiji Restoration, to becoming a global economic power post-World War II.

commentary.inflation_management: Japan spent most of the period fighting deflation: inflation was 0.3% in 2006, negative in 2009-11, and near zero through the 2010s despite the Bank of Japan's 2013 quantitative and qualitative easing and yield-curve control. The 2014 consumption-tax hike briefly lifted it to 2.8%. The global 2022 shock finally broke the deflationary mindset, with inflation reaching 2.5% in 2022, 3.3% in 2023, and a projected 3.2% in 2025, and the BOJ ended negative rates in March 2024. After decades of undershooting, Japan now faces the novel challenge of keeping inflation from overshooting while normalizing policy.
commentary.debt_management: Japan has the developed world's highest public debt: 152.1% of GDP in 2006, rising through the GFC (172.9% in 2009), the 2011 earthquake, and Abenomics-era stimulus to 206.3% in 2019, then 228.8% in 2020 on COVID, easing to a projected 206.5% in 2025. It has remained sustainable because it is overwhelmingly domestically held, the BOJ owns roughly half, and borrowing costs stayed near zero for years. In dollar terms GDP fell from $5.3tn (2012) to a projected $4.4tn (2025) on yen weakness, flattering the ratio. The risk is rising interest costs as rates normalize.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis hit exports hard; debt jumped past 170% of GDP.
Tohoku earthquake, tsunami, and Fukushima disaster; massive reconstruction spending followed.
Abenomics launched; BOJ began QQE in April 2013 targeting 2% inflation.
Consumption tax raised to 10%, denting demand just before COVID.
COVID-19; debt hit 228.8% of GDP on emergency spending.
Yen slid sharply; BOJ defended yield-curve control amid global tightening.
BOJ ended negative rates and YCC, beginning cautious normalization.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Japan's base case is low but positive growth with inflation settling near 2% and very gradual policy normalization. The debt trajectory depends on interest rates: sustained higher yields would eventually raise debt-service costs materially, though domestic ownership provides a deep buffer. Demographics remain the structural drag, partially offset by productivity gains and corporate reform. The analytical risk is a disorderly bond-market repricing if fiscal discipline slips; the upside is that escaping deflation durably would be a historic success.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
